stories.head: Trump and Putin shake hands in China ahead of three-way talks with Xi
stories.say: Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin shook hands in Shenzhen on Wednesday, their first meeting since August 2025, ahead of three-way talks with Xi Jinping on Thursday.
stories.stand: The leaders of the US, Russia and China are expected to meet on Thursday, with Ukraine and Iran on the agenda.
body: Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin shook hands on Wednesday, their first encounter since they met in Alaska in August 2025. Xi Jinping greeted Trump in Shenzhen with an airport ceremony including a red carpet and a military honour guard.

The three leaders are expected to meet on Thursday on the sidelines of the APEC forum. Euronews reports the agenda includes the war in Ukraine, the Iran conflict, nuclear proliferation, trade and artificial intelligence.
A US official told Al Jazeera that Trump and Putin will also hold a one-on-one meeting on Thursday. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected in Berlin the same day for Ukraine talks.

stories.head: Iran fires at Kuwait and Bahrain after US strike on Qeshm Island
stories.say: Iran fired on a US-used air base in Kuwait and on targets in Bahrain early on Wednesday, after a US strike on a missile site on Qeshm Island. Both countries say they intercepted the attacks.
stories.stand: Kuwait activated its air defences for the first time since early September as the exchange of fire in the Gulf widened.
body: Iran fired on the Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait and at US targets in Bahrain early on Wednesday. It followed a US strike on a Revolutionary Guard missile site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

The US said that strike answered an Iranian attack on a US radar installation in Bahrain on Tuesday. Iran said its attacks responded to US drone surveillance and an attack on Iranian communications towers.
Kuwait's army said it intercepted drones and reported no damage. Bahrain said it intercepted several attacks. Al Jazeera reports Bahrain has faced four Iranian attacks in six days.

Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the Arab League and the Gulf Cooperation Council condemned the attacks. UAE oil company ADNOC said one tanker crew member was missing and 11 injured after an attack in the strait.

stories.head: Israel launches first ground push in central Gaza since ceasefire
stories.say: Israeli tanks pushed into central Gaza on Wednesday near the Nuseirat and Bureij camps. Hospital officials say three Palestinians were killed; Hamas calls it a ceasefire breach.
stories.stand: The Israeli military says it is removing a threat near the Yellow Line; Hamas says the operation breaks the truce in place since October 2025.
body: Israel began a new military operation in central Gaza on Wednesday. Tanks were reported east of Nuseirat refugee camp and north of Bureij camp, and families fled northern Nuseirat.
Hospital officials said three Palestinians were killed in the operation. Israel's military said it aimed to remove a threat near the Yellow Line, which divides Israeli- and Hamas-controlled areas.
Hamas called the operation a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement. COGAT, the Israeli body for civilian affairs, told aid groups to avoid the area.

According to an AFP tally of health ministry figures, more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began. The Israeli military reports seven soldiers and one civilian contractor killed.

stories.head: Hegseth announces military cooperation deal on surprise Caracas visit
stories.say: Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Caracas on Wednesday and announced military cooperation with Venezuela's interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez.
stories.stand: The deal with Venezuela's interim government covers intelligence sharing and joint training, but no timeline has been published.
body: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a military cooperation agreement with Venezuela during an unannounced visit to Caracas on Wednesday. He met the interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez.
Al Jazeera reports the deal covers intelligence sharing and joint training. Euronews reports it also covers upgrading equipment. Neither government has published a timeline or the resources involved.

Rodríguez took office in January after a US-backed operation removed Nicolás Maduro. Hegseth said the shared aim was to stabilise Venezuela and remove drug-trafficking groups. He was due in Colombia later on Wednesday.

stories.head: Iraqi court jails six French nationals for life for joining Islamic State
stories.say: A court in Baghdad sentenced six French citizens to life in prison on Wednesday for joining Islamic State. They are among forty-seven French nationals moved from Syria to Iraq last year.
stories.stand: The six are among 47 French citizens transferred from Syria in 2025; rights groups have questioned whether such trials are fair.
body: A criminal court in Baghdad sentenced six French nationals to life in prison on Wednesday for joining the Islamic State group. Representatives of the French embassy attended.

The six are among 47 French citizens transferred from Syria to Iraq in 2025. Their trials began in September. One defendant, Thomas Barnouin, 45, told the court he went to Syria believing it was a religious duty.
Rights groups have criticised Iraqi terrorism trials as rushed and lacking due process. In February, Iraq received more than 5,700 Islamic State detainees from more than 60 countries.

stories.head: Russian strikes kill at least five in Ukraine, four of them in Odesa
stories.say: Russian air attacks killed at least five people across Ukraine on Wednesday, four of them in Odesa, where strikes hit the historic centre. Eighty settlements in Rivne lost power.
stories.stand: The attacks came a day after Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, and as the EU proposed a €45bn loan for Kyiv.
body: Russian air attacks across Ukraine killed at least five people on Wednesday. In Odesa, at least four were killed and 13 wounded, and regional head Oleg Kiper said three strikes hit the historic centre.
A drone strike killed a woman in the Zaporizhzhia region. In the Rivne region, 80 settlements lost power, with no casualties reported.

Ukraine's Energy Ministry says Russia has launched more than 1,000 attacks on energy infrastructure since September. The European Commission proposed a €45bn loan towards Ukraine's €70bn funding gap for next year.

stories.head: Bukele confirms Salvadoran air strike on Haitian gang leader's mansion
stories.say: El Salvador's president, Nayib Bukele, says his forces destroyed the mansion of Haitian gang leader Jeff Larose north of Port-au-Prince on Wednesday. It is unclear whether Larose was there.
stories.stand: Bukele posted video of helicopters firing on the house; it is not known whether the gang leader was inside.
body: El Salvador's president, Nayib Bukele, confirmed on Wednesday that his forces attacked and destroyed the mansion of Haitian gang leader Jeff Larose. The house is in Canaan, north of Port-au-Prince.
Bukele posted video on X showing Salvadoran helicopters firing on the property. It is unclear whether Larose was killed or was in the house.

Bukele deployed about 2,500 troops to Haiti last month. Another gang leader, Wilson Joseph of the 400 Mawozo gang, was targeted on 8 November. Experts quoted by AP warned of risks to civilians and of gang reprisals.

stories.head: Netanyahu ally ousted as Knesset speaker in 66-52 vote
stories.say: Israel's parliament elected Matan Kahana of Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party as speaker on Wednesday, by sixty-six votes to fifty-two, replacing Likud's Amir Ohana.
stories.stand: The vote gives Benjamin Netanyahu's opponents control of the agenda in parliament as Gadi Eisenkot tries to form a government.
body: Israel's 120-seat Knesset elected Matan Kahana as speaker by 66 votes to 52 on Wednesday. Kahana belongs to the centre-right Yashar party led by Gadi Eisenkot. He replaces Amir Ohana of Likud.
The speaker has strong influence over which bills come to a vote. Members of Eisenkot's bloc were also named to chair several key committees.

President Isaac Herzog has tasked Eisenkot with forming a government. Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister. ABC reports Likud's alliance holds 53 seats, Yashar and partners 48, and Arab-led parties 19.

stories.head: Bahrain jails 64 for life, mostly Shia clerics, over alleged Iran plot
stories.say: A court in Bahrain has jailed sixty-four people for life, most of them Shia clerics, over an alleged Iran-backed plot. Rights groups say confessions were forced.
stories.stand: Prosecutors say the defendants ran a group linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards; rights groups allege torture and forced confessions.
body: A court in Bahrain sentenced 64 people, most of them Shia clerics, to life in prison over an alleged Iran-backed plot to overthrow the government. Five others received 15-year terms.
Prosecutors say the defendants ran a terrorist group linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Senior Shia figure Sheikh Isa Qassim, who lives in Iran, was among those tried in absentia.

Twenty rights groups, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, say torture and forced confessions were used. Prosecutors deny that any rights were violated. Iran's foreign ministry condemned the ruling.

stories.head: Japan scrambles jets after suspected Russian planes enter its airspace
stories.say: Japan scrambled fighter jets on Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered its airspace near Fukuoka for about three minutes each. Tokyo has protested to Moscow.
stories.stand: Tokyo lodged a protest with Moscow ahead of an APEC summit both leaders are due to attend.
body: Japan said it scrambled fighter jets on Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered its airspace near Okinoshima, off the Fukuoka area. Each stayed in Japanese airspace for about three minutes.

Chief government spokesman Minoru Kihara called the violation completely unacceptable, and Japan lodged a protest with Moscow. South Korea said Russian aircraft entered its air defence zone earlier the same day but did not breach its airspace.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Vladimir Putin are both due at the APEC summit in Shenzhen this week. Russia's response was not reported.

stories.head: Saudi-led coalition says it hit 60 Houthi sites as fighting nears Aden
stories.say: The Saudi-led coalition says it struck sixty Houthi military targets in Yemen on Tuesday, including missile tunnels, as Houthi forces advanced towards Aden.
stories.stand: Government forces pulled back from the Bab al-Mandeb area to defend Aden, Al Jazeera reports.
body: The Saudi-led coalition said it struck 60 Houthi military targets on Tuesday, including tunnels used to build and store ballistic missiles. Spokesman Turki al-Maliki announced the strikes on Wednesday.
The strikes hit the Sanaa, Hodeidah, Amran and Saada governorates. Houthi forces meanwhile advanced towards Aden, the temporary seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government.

Al Jazeera reports government forces withdrew from Dhubab airport and the Bab al-Mandeb area to defend Aden. Fighting was also reported in Taiz. Saudi forces said they intercepted two Houthi cruise missiles aimed at Riyadh.

stories.head: Philippine police file child abuse material complaints against Thomas Markle
stories.say: Police in the Philippines have filed complaints against Thomas Markle, the Duchess of Sussex's father, recommending charges over child sexual abuse material. He denies all the claims.
stories.stand: Prosecutors in Cebu say the complaints will be reviewed; the 82-year-old has denied the allegations.
body: Philippine police have filed complaints against Thomas Markle, 82, the father of the Duchess of Sussex. They recommend two counts of distributing and one count of possessing child sexual abuse material.

The complaints were filed on Monday in Cebu province, where Markle reportedly lived for more than a year. Police said they recovered material from three memory cards and a phone at a former residence.
Prosecutor Graeme Elmido said the complaints would go through a preliminary evaluation. Markle has denied all the claims. Earlier this month he was charged in the US with one count of possession.

stories.head: Zelenskyy proposes 10 more evacuations from occupied areas
stories.say: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has proposed ten more evacuations from Russian-occupied areas, modelled on a truce in Oleshky that Melania Trump says let almost eight hundred people leave.
stories.stand: Ukraine will raise the plan with US mediators after a brief truce in Oleshky let residents leave through a safe corridor.
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has proposed 10 more humanitarian evacuations from Russian-occupied parts of the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions. He did not name the settlements.

The plan is modelled on a truce in Oleshky from 27 October to 1 November, which was initiated by Melania Trump. She said almost 800 people were evacuated. Ukraine's delegation will raise the proposal with US mediators.
Kyiv says Russia used the Oleshky truce to rotate troops.

stories.head: Bill to phase out leasehold enters Parliament with £250 ground rent cap
stories.say: A bill to phase out leasehold enters Parliament on Thursday. It would cap ground rents at two hundred and fifty pounds a year from 2028 and make commonhold the norm for new flats.
stories.stand: The government says the bill would cover about 5.1 million leasehold homes in England and Wales, if Parliament passes it.
body: The Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill enters Parliament on Thursday 19 November. The housing ministry says about 5.1 million homes in England and Wales are leasehold.

The bill would cap ground rents at £250 a year from 2028, falling to zero after 40 years. Commonhold would become the standard for most new flats, and existing blocks could convert with 50% support from neighbours, down from 100%.

It would also make lease extensions of 990 years easier and give ministers powers to cap excessive admin fees. Housing minister Matthew Pennycook called leasehold an anachronism. The changes need Parliament's approval and Royal Assent.

stories.head: UK house prices up 1.2% in a year as London falls 3.5%
stories.say: UK house prices rose one point two per cent in the year to September, to an average of two hundred and seventy-three thousand pounds. London prices fell three and a half per cent.
stories.stand: Official figures show prices dipped 0.5% in the month, with the North East leading annual growth.
body: The average UK house price was £273,000 in September, up 1.2% on a year earlier, according to the official UK House Price Index. Prices fell 0.5% from August.
In England the average was £293,000, up 0.8% in a year. In Wales it was £215,000, up 1.8%.
The North East had the strongest annual growth among English regions, at 4.6%. London had the weakest, with prices down 3.5% on a year earlier.

stories.head: Home Secretary announces about 200 Local Police Commands
stories.say: Shabana Mahmood has announced about two hundred Local Police Commands across England and Wales, each with a named commander, to focus on burglary, phone theft and antisocial behaviour.
stories.stand: The commands would form the base of a new three-layer policing structure, with a National Police Service at the top.
body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood announced on Wednesday around 200 new Local Police Commands across England and Wales. She set out the plan in a speech to police leaders.

The commands would focus on burglary, vehicle theft, phone theft and antisocial behaviour. Each would have a named commander accountable to local people, with boundaries broadly matching council areas.

Above them would sit specialist services for serious crime, and a National Police Service for national and international threats. The Home Office says cutting duplication across the current 43 force headquarters would free officers for neighbourhood work. No start date was given.

stories.head: US officer held in UK over suspected Russia spying moved to US custody
stories.say: A US Army lieutenant colonel arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of spying for Russia has been handed to US military custody. He has not been charged, and the Kremlin denies any link.
stories.stand: Counter-terrorism police held the officer under the National Security Act; he has not been charged.
body: A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been handed to US military custody, British and American officials said. Lieutenant Colonel Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested near Gloucester on 10 November.

He was held on suspicion of offences under the National Security Act 2023. Counter Terrorism Policing, which led the investigation with US authorities, said the country involved was Russia. He has not been charged.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor called the allegations extremely serious. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia had nothing to do with the case.

stories.head: Home Office targets 500 most persistent shoplifters
stories.say: The Home Office is targeting around five hundred of the most prolific shoplifters, with possible town centre bans, GPS tags and jail for breaches, starting with three police forces.
stories.stand: Up to 16 police forces will join the scheme, which has £2.5m of initial funding.
body: The Home Office has launched a drive against around 500 of the most persistent shop thieves in England and Wales. Up to 16 police forces will take part, starting with West Midlands, Merseyside and the Metropolitan Police.

Courts could order bans from high streets, GPS tags, more frequent supervision hearings and jail for breaking conditions. Foreign offenders could be referred to Immigration Enforcement. Support for drug and alcohol problems is also included.
The scheme has £2.5m in initial funding. The Home Office says shop theft is down 2% on last year. A 2025 pilot in Bromley targeting 10 offenders cut recorded retail crime by 70%, it says.

stories.head: £10,000 reward offered in hunt for man linked to attacks on Nottingham sex workers
stories.say: Police in Nottingham are hunting a man over nine offences against sex workers, including suspected rape. Crimestoppers is offering up to ten thousand pounds for information.
stories.stand: Nottinghamshire Police have released footage and an image of the man they want to trace.
body: Nottinghamshire Police want to speak to a man over nine offences against sex workers in the Forest Road West area of Nottingham. The offences took place between October 2025 and September 2026.
Police said their investigation identified five further potential assaults, including rape and attempted rape. The force has released footage and a still image.
Crimestoppers is offering up to £10,000 for information, given anonymously, that leads to an arrest and conviction. Detective Chief Inspector Ruby Burrow urged people to come forward even if unsure.

stories.stand: The message read out by Brand's wife prompted an investigation into whether he broke prison rules.
body: Labour deputy leader Lucy Powell said she was appalled that broadcasters aired a message from Russell Brand, who is serving ten and a half years for rape. Brand's wife read the message on a YouTube podcast on Sunday.

Powell told LBC that Brand shows no remorse. She also said the government is looking at the law on the age of sexual consent.

stories.stand: A yellow cold-health alert covers three northern regions of England until 9am on Thursday.

The RAC advised drivers to stick to major roads. A tree blocked the railway between Llandudno Junction and Holyhead, affecting Avanti West Coast and Transport for Wales.
The UK Health Security Agency has a yellow cold-health alert in place for the North West, North East, and Yorkshire and the Humber until 9am on Thursday.

stories.head: Bayesian sank after winds hit 68 knots in 14 minutes, investigators find
stories.say: Investigators say the yacht Bayesian sank in 2024 after calm weather turned to winds of at least sixty-eight knots in fourteen minutes. Seven people died.
stories.stand: The MAIB says the yacht's vulnerability to high winds at anchor had never been assessed, and the winds were not forecast.
body: The Marine Accident Investigation Branch published its report on the sinking of the yacht Bayesian on Thursday. Seven people died when it foundered off Porticello, Italy, on 19 August 2024. Fifteen survivors reached a liferaft.
Investigators found that calm conditions turned into winds of at least 68 knots within 14 minutes. Within 15 seconds the yacht was pushed onto its side.

The report says its vulnerability to high winds had gone unrecognised because it had never been assessed at anchor with sails down. The extreme winds were not explicitly forecast. Chief inspector Rob Loder said the accident developed with extraordinary speed.

stories.head: Aircraft return to RAF Brize Norton after 16-week runway rebuild
stories.say: Aircraft are flying again from RAF Brize Norton after its three-kilometre runway was fully replaced in sixteen weeks, part of a hundred and eighty million pound airfield programme.
stories.stand: The first aircraft landed on the new runway on 13 November, the Ministry of Defence says.
body: RAF Brize Norton's 3km runway has been fully replaced in 16 weeks, the Defence Infrastructure Organisation says. The first aircraft landed on the new surface on 13 November.
Aircraft were moved to other airfields during the work. The runway is part of a £180 million airfield programme due to finish in late 2027.
The new surface is designed to cope better with higher temperatures, and the concrete is expected to more than double the runway's service life.

stories.head: Tall ship breaks free in strong winds and blocks Douglas Harbour
stories.say: A French brigantine, La Malouine, broke free from its moorings in strong winds and blocked the entrance to Douglas Harbour on the Isle of Man overnight on Monday.
stories.stand: Emergency services attended and the harbour's lifting bridge has since reopened.
body: A tall ship broke free from its moorings in strong winds and blocked the entrance to Douglas Harbour on the Isle of Man overnight on Monday. Forecasters had warned of gusts up to 60mph.
The ship, La Malouine, is a French brigantine more than 60 years old, built in 1959 as an ice-breaking tug. It came to rest near the Millennium Lifting Bridge.
Emergency services attended and the bridge has since reopened, ITV News reports.

stories.head: Burnham says EU deal will put British young people first for jobs
stories.say: Andy Burnham says any new deal with the EU will put British young people first for jobs, ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday.
stories.stand: The prime minister spoke ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November that is expected to include a youth experience scheme.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that any deal with Europe would prioritise British young people for jobs. He told Good Morning Britain that closer ties with the EU would create opportunities for young people not in education, employment or training.
A UK-EU summit is due in Brussels on 20 November. The UK is seeking agreements on food, emissions trading and youth mobility, including a UK-EU Youth Experience scheme.

The number of young people not in education, employment or training topped one million earlier this year. Burnham called a review of youth unemployment by former health secretary Alan Milburn a watershed moment.

stories.head: UK pledges more than 1,000 long-range strike drones to Ukraine
stories.say: Britain is sending Ukraine more than a thousand long-range strike drones in a two hundred and sixty million pound package, announced as Andy Burnham arrived in Berlin.
stories.stand: The package is worth £260 million, with more than 80% of the money spent in the UK, the government says.
body: The UK will give Ukraine a £260 million package including more than 1,000 long-range strike drones able to fly more than 1,000km, the government said on Wednesday. Maritime, logistics and surveillance drones are also included.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced it as he arrived in Berlin to co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing. He then travels to Brussels for the UK-EU summit.
The government says more than 80% of the funding will be spent in the UK. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said Vladimir Putin uses winter as a weapon in Ukraine.

stories.head: Immigration and Asylum Bill clears Commons by 290 votes to 94
stories.say: The Immigration and Asylum Bill has cleared the Commons by two hundred and ninety votes to ninety-four. It would scrap notice periods before removing failed asylum seekers.
stories.stand: The bill now moves to the House of Lords; it would also define "bad faith" modern slavery claims in law.
body: The Immigration and Asylum Bill passed its Third Reading in the House of Commons by 290 votes to 94, the Home Office said on Wednesday. It now goes to the House of Lords.

The bill would scrap the notice period before failed asylum seekers are removed, giving officers a six-month window instead of the current five working days' notice. It would also create an Independent Immigration Appeals Authority.
It would define bad faith modern slavery claims in law and ask asylum seekers to contribute to support costs where they can. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is leading the bill.

stories.head: Chris Bryant calls Stormont ministers "commentators" as budget stalls
stories.say: Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant told MPs that Stormont ministers act like commentators rather than decision-makers, as the Executive's budget for this year remains stalled.
stories.stand: The UK has offered about £1.5bn over three years; the Executive says that is not enough.
body: Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant told MPs on Wednesday that Stormont ministers were acting as commentators rather than decision-makers. The Executive's 2026-27 budget has stalled.

Bryant told the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee the UK had offered about £1.5bn over three years, including £525m this year. The Executive says that is not enough, and its latest request was £1.5bn this year, Bryant said.

Departments are working on contingency budgets at 95% of last year's spending. On Thursday Bryant meets Irish ministers in Dublin at the British-Irish Intergovernmental Conference, where legacy of the Troubles is on the agenda.

stories.head: Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate seat, unseating Dan Sullivan
stories.say: Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's Senate seat, unseating Republican Dan Sullivan after a two-week count. It gives Democrats fifty-six of the hundred Senate seats.
stories.stand: Alaska was the last Senate race to be settled; Democrats will hold 56 seats to the Republicans' 44.
body: Democrat Mary Peltola has defeated Republican senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska, according to the official ballot count. Euronews reports she took 50.12% of the vote, with 144,302 votes to Sullivan's 131,844.
Counting took about two weeks after the 3 November vote because of Alaska's remote areas. It was the last Senate race to be decided.

Democrats will hold 56 of the 100 Senate seats. Peltola is one of the first two Native American women elected to the Senate. Federal investigators are looking into alleged voter confusion involving a second candidate named Dan Sullivan; Peltola denies any knowledge of it.

stories.say: House Democrats have chosen Hakeem Jeffries as their nominee for speaker, by two hundred and fifty-one votes to eleven. He would be the first Black speaker.
stories.stand: Jeffries still needs to win a vote of the full House when the new Congress meets on 3 January.
body: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries of New York for speaker on Wednesday, by 251 votes to 11 in a closed-door ballot. He would be the first Black speaker of the House.
Jeffries, 56, faced no declared challenger. Seven newly elected Democrats who opposed him cited unmet demands on Medicare for All, Al Jazeera reports.
He must still win a vote of the full House when the new Congress convenes on 3 January 2027. Democrats won control of both chambers in the midterm elections.

stories.say: Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, has told twelve people close to Donald Trump, including two of his sons, to preserve documents.
stories.stand: Robert Garcia is expected to chair the Oversight Committee when Democrats take the House in January.
body: Representative Robert Garcia, the senior Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has sent letters to 12 people telling them to preserve documents, CBS News reports.

Recipients include Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem and JD Vance. Garcia is expected to chair the committee when Democrats take control of the House in January.

The planned inquiries cover alleged corruption, conduct at the Department of Homeland Security and the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files. White House counsel Will Scharf warned the probes could cross legal lines; Garcia said Congress has wide latitude.

stories.say: A US judge has ordered Donald Trump to give sworn testimony in his defamation case against the BBC by the twenty-second of January, with both sides to be ready for trial by May.
stories.stand: Trump is seeking at least $5bn over the BBC's edit of his 6 January 2021 speech; the BBC denies he suffered real harm.
body: A US federal judge in Florida has ordered Donald Trump to give sworn deposition testimony in his defamation suit against the BBC by 22 January 2027. Judge Jeffrey T. Kuntz extended an earlier deadline of 11 December.
Both sides must be ready for trial by 3 May 2027. Trump says a Panorama documentary misleadingly joined two parts of his speech of 6 January 2021.
Trump is seeking at least $5bn on each of two claims; the judge has dismissed one of them. The BBC has apologised for the edit but denies Trump suffered any real harm.

stories.head: US lawmakers push bill to raise federal minimum wage to $25
stories.say: Seventeen US lawmakers are pushing a bill to lift the federal minimum wage from seven dollars twenty-five to twenty-five dollars an hour, and to end the lower wage for tipped workers.
stories.stand: The federal minimum has been $7.25 an hour since 2009; the bill would phase in the rise by 2038.
body: A group of 17 current and newly elected US lawmakers is pushing the Living Wage For All Act, Al Jazeera reports. It would gradually raise the federal minimum wage to $25 an hour.
Large employers would complete the rise by 2031 and smaller ones by 2038. The bill would also scrap the $2.13 an hour minimum for tipped workers.
The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since 2009. The bill was introduced in April and has stalled.

stories.say: The White House has pulled its nomination of Dr Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration, after senators from both parties questioned her views on vaccines.
stories.stand: Reports said she lacked the votes on the Senate health committee; its chair says she would have had them.
body: The White House withdrew the nomination of Dr Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration on Tuesday, ITV News reports, citing AP.

Committee chair Bill Cassidy wrote on X that she would have had the votes, and that the administration withdrew her rather than make commitments. Kyle Diamantas is acting head of the FDA.

stories.head: Cape Verde's President José Maria Neves re-elected with 63.8%
stories.say: José Maria Neves has been re-elected president of Cape Verde with sixty-three point eight per cent of the vote, according to provisional results from the electoral commission.
stories.stand: Provisional results show a clear win for the incumbent; about 150 international observers monitored the vote.
body: Cape Verde's president, José Maria Neves, won re-election in Sunday's vote with 63.8% of ballots cast, according to provisional results from the electoral commission.
Nearly 420,000 people were eligible to vote. Rival candidates included Joana Rosa Amado, the country's first woman presidential candidate.
Neves was first elected in 2021 and is backed by the PAICV, which won legislative elections in May. About 150 observers from ECOWAS, the African Union and the EU monitored the vote.

stories.head: UK inflation rises to 3.6% as fuel prices climb
stories.say: UK inflation rose to three point six per cent in October, the highest in a year. The Office for National Statistics says fuel prices were the biggest push.
stories.stand: It is the fourth monthly rise in a row; the ONS says motor fuel prices were up 33.2% on a year earlier.
body: UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.6% in October from 3.5% in September, the Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday. It is the highest rate in a year and the fourth monthly increase in a row.

The ONS said motor fuel prices were the biggest upward pressure, rising 33.2% over the year. ITV News reports the average petrol price rose 5.2p a litre between September and October. Restaurants and hotels pulled the rate down.
Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was 2.8%. The Bank of England expects inflation to peak just below 5% next spring, ITV News reports.

stories.stand: Ofgem confirms the January to March cap on 25 November; the forecast excludes a £100 government payment.
body: Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight forecasts that Ofgem's price cap will rise 26% to £2,166 a year from 1 January. That would be £443 more than the current level and the highest since 2023.
Cornwall Insight blamed events in the Middle East. Ofgem will announce the January to March cap on 25 November.
The forecast excludes a £100 energy payment for households in council tax bands A to D in England. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said affordability was her top priority.

stories.head: Jet2 cuts winter seats as Iran war pushes up jet fuel costs
stories.say: Jet2 has cut two hundred and forty thousand seats from its winter programme because of higher jet fuel costs. Half-year profit fell nineteen per cent, even as passenger numbers hit a record.
stories.stand: The holiday firm's half-year profit fell 19% to £652.2m while revenue and passenger numbers hit records.
body: Jet2 has cut its winter 2026-27 programme to manage higher jet fuel costs linked to the Iran war. Seat capacity has fallen by 240,000 since early September, a 3.6% drop on a year earlier.
In the six months to 30 September, pre-tax profit fell 19% to £652.2m. Revenue rose 5% to a record £5.63bn, and passengers rose 9% to 15.4 million.
The company declined to give full-year profit guidance, citing continued volatility in jet fuel prices. It said package pricing remained resilient.

stories.stand: The chipmaker forecast about $130bn in revenue next quarter, assuming no data centre chip sales to China.
body: Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8bn for the quarter to 25 October, up 103% on a year earlier and above Wall Street expectations. Net income was $65.3bn and data centre revenue more than doubled to $107.6bn.
The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of about $130bn, assuming no data centre chip sales to China. Its shares rose about 5% at one point in after-hours trading.

Board chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned as chief executive. Finance chief Colette Kress is interim chief executive. Huang is due to give a closed-door interview to Congress on 1 December.

stories.say: Iraq has restarted oil flows through its pipeline to Turkey, shut since 2014, giving it an export route that avoids the disrupted Strait of Hormuz.
stories.stand: The line can carry up to 750,000 barrels a day; Iraq plans to raise flows to 500,000 but has given no timetable.
body: Iraq resumed oil flows through the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline to Turkey on Tuesday, after tests by the Oil Ministry. The line had been shut since 2014 after Islamic State attacks.
It gives Iraq an export route that avoids the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has been disrupted by the Iran war. Oil runs from northern Iraq to Ceyhan on Turkey's Mediterranean coast.
Initial flow is 120,000 barrels a day, with a planned increase to 500,000 and no timetable. The pipeline can carry up to 750,000 barrels a day.

stories.stand: Other estimates put the cost far lower, and shipping traffic through the strait is about 65% below pre-war levels.
body: Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao told a Senate confirmation hearing on Tuesday that insurance for a single Strait of Hormuz transit now costs $64m. He said the pre-war cost was $54,000. Al Jazeera says the figure has not been independently verified.
Other estimates are lower. A Reuters report in September put the cost of moving an oil cargo through the strait at about $10m to $20m.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre recorded 308 crossings in the seven days to 11 November, about 65% below pre-war levels.

stories.stand: The bank says the matters in the leaked files date back many years and that no account or payment data was accessed.
body: The data protection office in the German state of Hesse has opened an investigation into Deutsche Bank after a leak of more than 15 million internal records. Commissioner Alexander Rossnagel will examine whether the bank protected the data and notified those affected promptly.
Media reports based on the leaked documents say the bank ignored internal warnings about money laundering and sanctions violations. Euronews says it has not verified those claims.

Deutsche Bank says the matters date back many years and that it has strengthened its controls. It says no account data, login details or payment data were accessed. Its share price has fallen since the leak.

stories.head: Gold hits lowest price since October 2025 as rate rise bets grow
stories.say: Gold fell on Monday to its lowest price since October 2025, and is down more than thirty per cent from January's record, as markets bet on a US rate rise.
stories.stand: Gold is on course for its biggest annual fall since 2015; silver is down about 60% from its peak.
body: Spot gold fell to $3,832 an ounce on Monday, its lowest since October 2025, before recovering slightly on Tuesday. Silver dropped to $46.50 an ounce.
Gold is down more than 30% from its January record of about $5,600 and is on track for its biggest annual fall since 2015. Silver is down about 60% from its peak.
Euronews attributes the slide to a strong dollar, high bond yields and expectations of a US interest rate rise in December. Goldman Sachs cut its year-end gold forecast to $4,150.

stories.say: Finnish satellite firm Iceye has bid two billion euros for Italian rocket maker Avio. Any deal needs regulatory approval.
stories.stand: Iceye also pledged €1bn of investment in Italy over five years; Avio's largest shareholder is Italy's Leonardo.
body: Finnish satellite operator Iceye has offered €2bn for Italian rocket maker Avio, it announced on Tuesday. It is offering €41 a share for all of Avio's ordinary shares.
Iceye also pledged €1bn of investment in Italy over five years. Its chief executive, Rafal Modrzewski, said governments need control of critical space infrastructure.
Avio's largest shareholder is Leonardo, which owns 18%. The Italian state holds about 30% of Leonardo, and any deal needs regulatory approval.

stories.head: EU economy beats forecasts but inflation stays higher for longer
stories.say: The European Commission has raised its EU growth forecast for this year to one point four per cent, but expects inflation to stay above three per cent into 2027.
stories.stand: The Commission's autumn forecast raised growth estimates but sees energy costs keeping inflation high into 2027.
body: The European Commission's autumn forecast, published on Tuesday, sees EU growth of 1.4% in 2026, up from the 1.1% it predicted in May. Eurozone growth is forecast at 1.2% in both 2026 and 2027.
EU inflation is forecast at 3.3% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027. The Commission expects it to peak above 4% around the turn of the year and fall to 2.3% in 2028.
Economy commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said the economy was holding up better than expected but warned the progress could not be taken for granted.

stories.head: CMA investigates Bannatyne, Secret Escapes and Caledonian over hidden fees
stories.say: The Competition and Markets Authority is investigating Bannatyne, Secret Escapes and Caledonian Leisure over fees added after the headline price.
stories.stand: The watchdog has reached no conclusions; it can fine firms up to 10% of global turnover.
body: The Competition and Markets Authority has opened investigations into three travel and leisure businesses over suspected drip pricing, it said on Wednesday. Drip pricing is when mandatory charges are added after the headline price.
The firms are gym chain Bannatyne Health Club, coach holiday company Caledonian Leisure and travel deals site Secret Escapes. The CMA has reached no conclusions.

Under consumer law the CMA can order compensation and fine firms up to 10% of global turnover. It says cases against 23 businesses since April 2025 have led to £2.3m in refunds and more than £12m in fines.

stories.head: Voyager 1 reaches one light day from Earth as engineers chase data fault
stories.say: Voyager 1 was due to reach one light day from Earth on Wednesday, the farthest any spacecraft has gone. But it stopped sending data last week, and engineers are investigating.
stories.stand: The probe launched in 1977 is the farthest human-made object from Earth; its signal still arrives but carries no data.
body: NASA's Voyager 1 was expected to reach one light day from Earth early on Wednesday, more than 16 billion miles away. No human-made object has travelled farther. The team plans to confirm the milestone on Thursday.

NASA says the spacecraft stopped sending science and engineering data on 14 November. A Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra still picked up its carrier signal, suggesting the fault lies in the computer that formats data.
Diagnosis could take weeks, NASA says, because each radio signal takes about 24 hours to travel each way. Voyager 1 launched in 1977 and travels at nearly 38,000mph, CBS News reports.

stories.head: Iron Age bog woman found in Northern Ireland was beheaded
stories.say: An Iron Age woman whose remains were found in a Northern Ireland bog was beheaded from behind, possibly in a ritual killing, an investigation has found.
stories.stand: The remains date from between 343 and 1 BC; no skull has been recovered.
body: An investigation hosted by the Ulster Museum has found that the Iron Age woman known as the Ballymacombs More Woman was beheaded, CBS News reports. She was decapitated from behind, probably with a bladed weapon, possibly in a ritual killing.
Her remains were found in a peat bog in central Northern Ireland in October 2023. They date from between 343 and 1 BC, and she was 15 to 22 years old when she died.
No skull has been recovered. An osteoarchaeologist found cut marks on the neck. The findings were presented through a public coroner-style investigation.

stories.head: Fossil teeth suggest Homo erectus lived in rainforests in southern China
stories.say: Fossil teeth found in caves in southern China suggest the ancient human species Homo erectus lived in rainforests, two studies in Nature say.
stories.stand: Two studies in Nature date the teeth to between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago, younger than any previous Homo erectus fossil in China.
body: Researchers have identified eight Homo erectus teeth and one from an unidentified ancient human in two caves near Chongzuo in southern China. They say the teeth show the species lived in rainforests.
The sediment holding the teeth is dated to between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago, ABC News reports. The previous youngest Homo erectus fossil in China was about 400,000 years old.

The work, by Australian, Chinese and European researchers, is published in two studies in Nature. Chemical analysis suggests one individual ate food from about 250km away as a child, in what is now Vietnam.

stories.head: NASA data confirms a first-of-its-kind star merger in Andromeda
stories.say: Astronomers using the James Webb telescope say a star smaller than the Sun spiralled into a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy and merged with it, a first.
stories.stand: The merged star, nicknamed Bao, is described in a study published in Nature.
body: Astronomers say a star slightly less massive than the Sun spiralled into a supergiant star in the Andromeda galaxy and merged with it, NASA reports. The merged object, AT 2025abao, is nicknamed Bao.
The James Webb Space Telescope observed it on 24 December 2025, about 47 days after its eruption peaked. Data also came from other telescopes, including Swift and Gemini North.
Before the merger the larger star had about seven times the Sun's mass. The two stars orbited each other for about seven years before merging. The study is published in Nature.

stories.head: Scientists debate whether near-Earth object is a lost Soviet probe
stories.say: Some researchers suggest a small object passing near Earth could be a Soviet probe lost in 1988. Others think it's a natural rock, and NASA says there's no cause for concern.
stories.stand: NASA says it is monitoring the 11-metre object and there is no evidence it could hit Earth.
body: Object 1998 KY26, about 11 metres wide, is passing near Earth, Euronews reports. Its path suggests forces other than gravity are acting on it.

Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb and two colleagues suggest it could be Phobos 1, a Soviet probe launched in July 1988 that lost contact on its way to Mars. Other studies point to a natural rocky body.
NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said the agency is monitoring the object and there is no evidence it could hit Earth. Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft is due to reach it in July 2031.

stories.head: SpaceX catches returning Starship with launch tower arms
stories.say: SpaceX caught its Starship spacecraft with the mechanical arms of its launch tower in Texas on Saturday, after a twenty-two hour flight. The booster exploded shortly after Friday's lift-off.
stories.stand: It is the first midair capture of a Starship returning from space, though a planned double catch did not happen.
body: SpaceX caught its Starship spacecraft with the mechanical arms of its launch tower at Starbase, Texas, on Saturday, Euronews reports. It describes it as the first successful midair capture of a Starship returning from space.
The spacecraft completed a 22-hour journey before descending upright to the tower. A planned double catch did not happen, because the first-stage booster exploded shortly after Friday's lift-off.
Starship is central to NASA's Artemis Moon missions. SpaceX plans to launch it from Kennedy Space Center in Florida in the coming months.

stories.say: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has sent its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, where NASA's DART probe struck the moonlet Dimorphos in 2022.
stories.stand: Detailed images of both asteroids are due on 25 November, the mission team says.
body: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos binary asteroid system, ScienceDaily reports. Principal investigator Patrick Michel said the larger asteroid's far side shows multiple boulders and craters.
NASA's DART spacecraft hit the smaller asteroid, Dimorphos, on 26 September 2022. The impact shortened its orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes.
Didymos is about 780m across and Dimorphos about 151m. Detailed images of both are scheduled for 25 November.

stories.head: NASA finds clues to ancient ice beyond Neptune in stratospheric dust
stories.say: NASA scientists say twelve tiny dust particles collected high above Earth point to an ancient ice reservoir in the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune, enriched in heavier forms of oxygen.
stories.stand: The particles were collected from the stratosphere by NASA's ER-2 high-altitude aircraft.
body: Scientists at NASA's Johnson Space Center analysed 12 tiny dust particles collected from Earth's stratosphere by the ER-2 high-altitude aircraft. NASA says they show evidence of an ancient ice reservoir in the Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune.
The ice was enriched in heavier oxygen isotopes. Tracks left by solar particles helped link the dust to the Kuiper Belt. UCLA contributed an ion microprobe to the work.
NASA says the scarcity of similar signatures in meteorites suggests giant planets may have limited mixing between the outer and inner solar system.

stories.head: Hippos roamed a lake in today's Arabian desert 125,000 years ago
stories.say: Archaeologists have found a hundred-and-twenty-five-thousand-year-old lakeside site in southern Saudi Arabia, with fossils of hippos and buffaloes and more than five thousand stone tools.
stories.stand: The study in Science describes an ancient lake of about 340 square kilometres in the Mundafan region.
body: Archaeologists have found a lakeside site about 125,000 years old in the Mundafan region of southern Saudi Arabia, ScienceDaily reports. It shows the area was once green.
The ancient lake covered about 340 square kilometres and was up to 29m deep. Fossils include hippos, extinct long-horned buffaloes, camels and gazelles. Researchers found 5,511 stone tools.

Plant residues on tools suggest some stone points were used as weapons. The authors call the idea of poisoned weapons tentative. The study, led by Griffith University and KAUST, is published in Science.

stories.head: Researchers build rechargeable battery using vitamin B12 as catalyst
stories.say: Spanish researchers have built a rechargeable zinc-air battery that uses vitamin B12 as a catalyst. The prototype lasted up to two hundred and fifty charge cycles.
stories.stand: The research-stage battery uses a water-based, non-flammable electrolyte.
body: Researchers at the University of Córdoba in Spain have built a research-stage rechargeable zinc-air battery that uses vitamin B12 as a catalyst, ScienceDaily reports.
The battery makes electricity from zinc and oxygen from the air. The vitamin's cobalt atom drives the reactions, and the water-based electrolyte is non-flammable.
The prototype survived up to 250 charge and discharge cycles. The work is published in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A.

stories.head: Thousands of tiny animals found living inside deep-sea nodules
stories.say: Researchers in Bremen found more than four thousand tiny animals living inside deep-sea metal nodules from the Pacific, the rocks targeted by deep-sea mining.
stories.stand: One nodule from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone held 245 animals, most under a millimetre long.
body: Researchers at the University of Bremen examined 244 polymetallic nodules from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the central Pacific. They found 4,139 animals living in cracks and cavities, an average of 17 per nodule. One nodule held 245.
Most of the animals are under a millimetre long. The communities differed from those in the surrounding mud and were similar across sites up to 1,000km apart.

The nodules lie at depths of 4,000 to 6,000m and are a target for mining of nickel, cobalt and copper. Professor Sabine Gollner warned mining could cause irreversible loss of unique biodiversity. The study is in Scientific Reports.

stories.head: Study suggests why over a billion years vanished from Earth's rock record
stories.say: University of Wollongong researchers say slow movements in Earth's mantle may explain the Great Unconformity, a gap in the rock record that spans up to more than a billion years.
stories.stand: Simulations published in Nature suggest mantle convection lifted ancient continents so erosion stripped away rock.
body: Researchers at the University of Wollongong say mantle convection may explain the Great Unconformity, ScienceDaily reports. It is a gap in Earth's rock record where 540 million-year-old rocks sit directly on much older rock.

Their simulations suggest the mantle slowly raised ancient continental cores, and erosion stripped away rock during the uplift. The missing time ranges from about 200 million years to more than a billion years.
The study is published in Nature. The authors say mantle convection may not be the only factor.

stories.head: Review finds brain tumour patients harmed by years of chemotherapy at Coventry trust
stories.say: A review found brain tumour patients at a Coventry hospital trust were harmed by years of repeated chemotherapy against guidelines. Six cases involved severe harm.
stories.stand: The trust has apologised and widened its historical review back to 2005; lawyers for more than 40 patients want a public inquiry.
body: A Royal College of Physicians review found that patients with brain tumours at University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust were severely harmed, ITV News reports. A consultant oncologist kept them on repeated cycles of the chemotherapy drug temozolomide for years, contrary to national guidelines.

Of 20 cases reviewed, 15 received unsatisfactory care. Six involved severe harm, five moderate harm and eight low harm. One patient received more than 100 cycles over 13 years before their diagnosis was found to be wrong.

The trust's chief executive, Professor Andy Hardy, apologised and extended its review of past cases back to 2005. A law firm representing more than 40 patients is calling for an independent public inquiry.

stories.stand: The true number is likely higher, because some trusts gave only approximate figures.
body: Seventy-nine NHS trusts in England recorded 3,029 incidents of staff improperly accessing patient records between 2021/22 and 2025/26, ITV News reports. The figures came from Freedom of Information requests by the PA news agency.

stories.say: Yvette Cooper has announced Neighbourhood Support Teams to manage the care of frail patients in England and keep them out of hospital.
stories.stand: At least half a million people should get support by April 2027, the government says.
body: Health and Social Care Secretary Yvette Cooper announced Neighbourhood Support Teams on Wednesday in a speech at the King's Fund. They would give frail or vulnerable patients dedicated care management to keep them out of hospital.
The government says at least 1% of England's population, more than half a million people, will get support by April 2027. It is aiming to reach nearly 2 million patients in later years.
Officials estimate net savings of more than £1bn a year. Up to 300,000 people are to get proactive GP support this winter under a £40m programme.

stories.say: Under new government plans, councils in England would arrange home care by neighbourhood, with one or two main providers each, so people see more familiar carers and care workers drive less.
stories.stand: Guidance and toolkits are due in the spring; a Bristol trial cut driving by 65%, the government says.

stories.stand: The researchers call the lack of oversight a gap in regulation and a patient safety issue.
body: Researchers at the University of St Andrews analysed 50 health tests advertised online and sold by retailers and clinics, Euronews reports. The study is published in BMJ Open.

stories.head: Viagra-family drug slows Alzheimer's decline in late-stage trial, developer says
stories.say: A drug from the same family as Viagra slowed decline by thirty-one per cent in a late-stage Alzheimer's trial, its developer AriBio says. Experts want more research.
stories.stand: Results in a wider group were not statistically significant, and experts say more research is needed.
body: South Korean company AriBio says its experimental tablet AR1001 slowed cognitive decline and memory loss by 31% in a Phase 3 trial, Euronews reports. The main group was 604 people with early Alzheimer's who were not on other treatments.
The drug belongs to the same class as Viagra and works by increasing blood flow to the brain. In a wider group also taking other drugs, the results were not statistically significant, AriBio said.
Results were presented at a conference in the US. Side effects were mostly mild to moderate. The Alzheimer's Society warned people against taking Viagra to treat Alzheimer's.

stories.head: Drug-resistant infections rising in Europe, ECDC warns
stories.say: The EU's disease agency says drug-resistant infections kill more than thirty-five thousand people a year in Europe, and resistant E. coli cases are rising, not falling.
stories.stand: The EU agency says Europe is missing its targets, with a 72% rise in one resistant bacterium since 2019.
body: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control says more than 35,000 people die each year from antimicrobial resistance in the EU, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway, Euronews reports.
Resistant E. coli infections rose 16.4% from 2019 to 2025, against a target of a 10% cut. The rate of resistant K. pneumoniae rose 72% over the same period.
The agency says more than 70% of the burden comes from multidrug-resistant infections picked up in healthcare settings, and half could be prevented.

stories.head: Brain's night-time cleaning waves weaken with age, MIT study finds
stories.say: An MIT study found the fluid waves that clean the brain during deep sleep are much smaller in older adults, though some match younger people.
stories.stand: The study compared people aged 18 to 39 with people aged 60 to 84.
body: Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that the brain's night-time waste-clearing system weakens with age, ScienceDaily reports.

Waves of cerebrospinal fluid during deep sleep were substantially smaller in older adults, linked to weaker slow brain waves. The study compared people aged 18 to 39 with people aged 60 to 84. Some older adults matched younger levels.
The study, led by Laura Lewis, is published in Nature Aging.

stories.head: Magnetic nanoparticles ease Parkinson's-like symptoms in mice
stories.say: Researchers say tiny magnetic particles in the brains of mice with Parkinson's-like damage eased movement problems when a magnetic field was applied.
stories.stand: The researchers say the effect is roughly comparable to deep brain stimulation, without implanted wires.
body: Researchers injected magnetic nanoplatelets into the brains of mice with Parkinson's-like damage, ScienceDaily reports. When an external magnetic field was applied, movement problems improved significantly.

The particles turn magnetic fields into tiny forces that open pressure-sensitive channels in nearby nerve cells. Researcher Danijela Gregurec said the effect was roughly comparable to deep brain stimulation.
No inflammation appeared over several months. The work, by teams in Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium, was in mice only and is published in Advanced Science.

stories.head: Rare inflammatory disease driven by natural killer cells, study finds
stories.say: Australian scientists say a rare inflammatory disease is driven mainly by faulty natural killer cells, challenging about thirty years of research.
stories.stand: A drug tested in one severely affected infant improved their condition, a result the team calls preliminary.
body: Scientists at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research found that mevalonate kinase deficiency, a rare inflammatory genetic disorder, is driven mainly by malfunctioning natural killer cells, ScienceDaily reports.
That challenges about 30 years of research that focused on other immune cells called macrophages. About half of patients do not respond well to current treatments.
The JAK inhibitor baricitinib improved the condition of one severely affected infant, a result the researchers describe as preliminary. The study is published in Immunity.

stories.head: Immune cells in fat behave differently in males and females, mouse study finds
stories.say: A mouse study found immune cells in fat behave differently in males and females, which may help explain why obesity affects the sexes differently.
stories.stand: The study identified six types of eosinophil in fat tissue; work in humans has not yet been done.
body: Researchers at the University of California, Riverside found that immune cells called eosinophils behave differently in fat tissue depending on their type and the sex of the animal, ScienceDaily reports. They identified six distinct populations.
Female mice had a protective group of eosinophils. Male mice on a high-fat diet more often developed populations linked to inflammation.
The study was in mice. Eosinophils have been found in human fat, but their role there is not yet understood. The work is published in PNAS Nexus.

stories.stand: The study reanalysed existing brain scans and is published in The Journal of Neuroscience.

The study is published in The Journal of Neuroscience. The report does not give the number of participants.

stories.head: COP31 talks deadlocked on finance and fossil fuels as deadline nears
stories.say: With COP31 in Antalya due to close on Friday, twenty-one issues remain unresolved, including finance and the move away from fossil fuels. Ministers held closed-door talks on Wednesday.
stories.stand: Observers expect the summit in Türkiye to run at least one night beyond its scheduled close on Friday.
body: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, is due to close on Friday with 21 issues unresolved, UN News reports. They include finance, adaptation and how fast the world moves away from fossil fuels. New draft texts are due early on Thursday.
Ministers held closed-door talks on Wednesday evening, chaired by COP31 president Murat Kurum. Climate Home News reports the Arab Group and Russia reject the draft cover decision.

A pledging session on Tuesday produced $50m for the Adaptation Fund, against an annual target of $300m. The second Global Stocktake, a five-yearly review of national climate pledges, was launched on Wednesday.

stories.head: EU carbon market reform softened in latest Council draft
stories.say: A new EU Council draft would let industrial firms keep eighty per cent of their free carbon allowances just by submitting an investment plan, even if they do not carry it out.
stories.stand: Campaigners say the changes put the EU's 2040 climate target at risk; ministers aim to agree on 11 December.
body: The Irish Presidency of the EU Council has softened a proposal to reform the Emissions Trading System, Euronews reports. EU ambassadors were due to discuss it on Wednesday.
Under the draft, industrial firms would keep 80% of free allowances if they submit an investment plan, even if they do not carry it out. The remaining 20% would depend on starting eligible projects.
The Presidency aims for agreement at the Environment Council on 11 December. An analysis for WWF Germany called the Commission's reform incompatible with a 90% net emissions cut by 2040.

stories.stand: Heatwaves caused almost 70% of the deaths, and the toll is likely an undercount, the report says.

Jamaica, Sri Lanka and Spain were the most affected countries in 2025. Spain's heatwave caused about 3,900 official deaths, and it had its worst wildfire season in three decades.

stories.say: A UNESCO and UCL report found AI models got about ninety per cent of neutral climate questions right, but usually changed their answer at the first sign of pushback.
stories.stand: The study, presented at COP31, tested up to 33 leading models across 13 languages.
body: A report by UNESCO and University College London found that AI models answered about 90% of neutral climate questions correctly, Euronews reports. It was presented at COP31 in Antalya.
But in eight of ten cases, models changed their answer at the first sign of mild disagreement, including confirming a false claim about carbon dioxide.
When judging how well climate policies work together, average accuracy was 33.8%, barely above chance. Up to 33 models were tested across 13 languages.

stories.stand: About three million residential heat pumps were installed in Europe in 2025, one million short of the Commission's target.
body: The European Heat Pump Association says heat pumps in every building and compatible industrial process, powered by renewables, would avoid around 600 million tonnes of CO2. That is more than Germany's emissions.
Each residential heat pump displaces about two tonnes of CO2 a year on average if its electricity is renewable, the group says.
Europe has about 30 million residential heat pumps. About three million were added in 2025, one million fewer than the European Commission's target of four million.

stories.say: A bacterium has killed about a third of the olive trees in Italy's Apulia region, and some farmers are planting thirsty avocados instead.
stories.stand: Reservoirs in part of the region are below 30% of capacity as farmers turn to a water-hungry crop.
body: Xylella fastidiosa, a bacterium first detected in Apulia in 2013, has killed about a third of the region's 60 million olive trees, Euronews reports. Damage so far is put at about €1bn.
Some farmers in Salento are replacing olives with avocados. Avocado trees can use up to 220 litres of water a day in summer.
Reservoirs in the Capitanata area are below 30% of capacity. The University of Bari estimates 23,885 hectares of affected groves could suit avocados.

stories.stand: The statewide map has a resolution of one square metre per pixel, NASA says.
body: NASA researchers have produced detailed 3D maps of the whole of California, down to the scale of a single tree, to help assess wildfire risk.

The team combined airborne lidar data from the US Geological Survey into one statewide map, with a resolution of one square metre per pixel. Most space-based lidar data are 10 to 25 square metres per pixel.
The work was done with California's Natural Resources Agency and Air Resources Board, and the data is available online.
